w1.title: Worked Example 1: Degree of a Polynomial & Geometrical Meaning of Zeros
w1.question: If the parabola y = p(x) crosses the x-axis at x = −2 and x = 3, what are its zeros?

steps.text: Zeros occur where y = p(x) = 0, which means points on the x-axis.
Read the x-coordinates of the x-axis intersections: (−2, 0) and (3, 0).
Therefore, the two zeros of p(x) are −2 and 3.

check.q: At most how many real zeros can a quadratic polynomial (degree 2) have?

opts.m: A degree-n polynomial can cross the x-axis at most n times.
A linear polynomial has 1 zero; a quadratic has 0, 1, or 2 real zeros.

w2.title: Worked Example 2: Sum & Product of Zeros (α + β = −b/a, αβ = c/a)
w2.question: Find the sum and product of the zeros of p(x) = x² − 5x + 6.

steps.text: Compare x² − 5x + 6 with ax² + bx + c: here a = 1, b = −5, c = 6.
Product of zeros: αβ = c/a = 6/1 = 6 (zeros are 2 and 3).

check.q: For 2x² + 8x + 6, what is the sum of its zeros?

opts.m: Do not forget the minus sign in −b/a = −8/2 = −4.
3 is the product of zeros (c/a = 6/2), not the sum.

w3.title: Worked Example 3: Forming a Quadratic Polynomial from Given Zeros
w3.question: Write a quadratic polynomial whose zeros have sum 4 and product 3.

steps.text: Given sum S = 4 and product P = 3.

check.q: Which quadratic polynomial has sum of zeros = 7 and product of zeros = 10?

opts.m: The middle term uses minus the sum: x² − (α+β)x + αβ.
Keep sum as the coefficient of −x and product as the constant term.

steps.title: Degree of a Polynomial & Geometrical Meaning of Zeros
steps.body: The degree of a polynomial p(x) is the highest power of x. Geometrically, the real zeros of p(x) are the x-coordinates where the graph y = p(x) intersects the x-axis.

steps.title: Forming a Quadratic Polynomial from Given Zeros
steps.body: Given the sum S = α + β and product P = αβ of zeros, a quadratic polynomial is formed by p(x) = x² − Sx + P.
